title: Police Officer Salary Victoria: Hourly to Annual Guide
description: Convert police officer salary Victoria from hourly to annual. See the 38-hour week, fortnight pay, tax, and super. Compare with state averages and minimum wage.
salarySummary: Based on a 38-hour week, a police officer's annual salary is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top at 12%.

faqs.q: How do I convert a police officer's hourly rate to annual salary in Victoria?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52. For a standard full-time role, assume 38 hours per week. For example, $40 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $79,040 per year before tax and super. Super is paid on top at 12% of ordinary earnings.

faqs.q: What is the fortnightly pay for a police officer in Victoria?
faqs.a: Fortnightly pay is the weekly pay multiplied by 2. If the weekly pay is hourly rate × 38 hours, then fortnightly pay is that amount × 2. For a $40/hour rate, weekly pay is $1,520, so fortnightly pay is $3,040 before tax and super.

faqs.q: How does the National Minimum Wage compare to a police officer salary in Victoria?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week, or $1,004.90 per week. Police officer salaries are typically higher and set by enterprise agreements. The Victorian full-time average weekly earnings (May 2026) were $2,041.10 per week, which is a state average, not a police-specific median.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Police Officer Salary Victoria

Police officer salaries in Victoria are generally determined by enterprise agreements and awards, not a single national rate. While the [National Minimum Wage](/topics/minimum-wage) sets a legal floor, most police officers earn well above that. This guide helps you convert an hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures, and explains how tax and super affect take-home pay.

### The Basic Conversion Formula

To estimate annual gross pay, use:

**Annual gross = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time police officer, we assume a standard 38-hour week (the typical full-time hours under the Fair Work Act). If you work different hours, adjust accordingly. This formula assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

For example, if your hourly rate is $45:
- Weekly: $45 × 38 = $1,710
- Fortnightly: $1,710 × 2 = $3,420
- Annual: $1,710 × 52 = $88,920

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many employers pay fortnightly. Knowing your fortnightly amount helps with budgeting. Simply double your weekly pay. Using the example above, $1,710 per week becomes $3,420 per fortnight before deductions.

### Tax on Police Officer Salaries

Tax is withheld from each pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus, the Medicare levy generally adds 2% (using 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). For a $88,920 annual salary, tax would be approximately:
- $0 on first $18,200
- 15% on $26,800 ($18,201–$45,000) = $4,020
- 30% on $43,920 ($45,001–$88,920) = $13,176
- Total tax ≈ $17,196
- Medicare levy (2% of $88,920) ≈ $1,778
- Total deductions ≈ $18,974

Take-home pay would be roughly $69,946 per year, or $1,345 per week. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a detailed estimate.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Employers must pay super guarantee at 12% of ordinary earnings (from 1 July 2026) on top of your salary. This is not deducted from your pay. For $88,920 annual salary, super is $10,670.40 per year, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award vs Enterprise Agreement

The [National Minimum Wage](/topics/minimum-wage) from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour ($1,004.90 per week for 38 hours). Casual employees receive 25% loading, making it $33.05 per hour. Police officers are typically permanent full-time, so casual loading does not apply.

Police officer pay is usually set by the Victorian Police Enterprise Agreement or an award. These rates are higher than the minimum wage. For context, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult ordinary time earnings in Victoria averaged $2,041.10 per week in May 2026. That is a state average for all full-time workers, not a police officer median. Individual police salaries vary by rank, experience, and allowances.

### Using the Hourly to Annual Calculator

Our [the timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate. If you are a casual employee, check the box to add 25% casual loading on top. Do not enter a rate that already includes loading. The calculator then shows annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures, plus estimated tax and super.

### Key Points to Remember

- Annual pay = hourly × hours per week × 52 (assume 38 hours for full-time)
- Fortnightly = weekly × 2
- Super is 12% paid on top, not deducted
- Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale plus Medicare
- The National Minimum Wage is a floor; police officer salaries are typically higher
- Victoria's average full-time weekly earnings ($2,041.10) is a state average, not a police-specific figure

For more detailed award information, see [pay guides](/blog) and [reference tables](/data). For hourly conversion tips, visit [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion).

### Disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
